overview.what_it_is: Re-tell Lecture is an integrated listening-and-speaking task in which the test taker listens to an academic lecture, identifies its central message and important supporting ideas, and then reconstructs the lecture orally in a clear, connected response. The goal is not to repeat every sentence or reproduce the speaker's exact words. The learner must show understanding by selecting useful information, organizing it logically, and delivering it fluently in their own words.

format_facts.label: Item type
format_facts.value: A long-answer speaking task based on a recorded academic lecture.

format_facts.label: Recording start
format_facts.value: The lecture begins automatically after a short three-second preview period.

format_facts.label: Image support
format_facts.value: Some items include an image that may help the learner predict the topic before the lecture begins.

format_facts.label: Preparation time
format_facts.value: After the lecture finishes, the learner has 10 seconds to review notes and prepare the opening.

format_facts.label: Response time
format_facts.value: The microphone opens automatically and the learner has up to 40 seconds to speak.

format_facts.label: Listening condition
format_facts.value: The lecture should be treated as a one-play recording, so attention and efficient note taking are essential.

format_facts.label: Response goal
format_facts.value: Retell the topic, main supporting ideas, important relationships, and any conclusion or implication.

scoring_factors.name: Content
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: How accurately and sufficiently the response communicates the lecture's main subject, central ideas, relevant developments, examples, relationships, conclusions, or implications.

scoring_factors.name: Oral Fluency
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether the response is delivered at a smooth and natural rate with connected phrasing, suitable rhythm, controlled pauses, and minimal hesitation or repetition.

scoring_factors.name: Pronunciation
scoring_factors.what_it_measures: Whether vowels, consonants, word stress, phrase stress, and intonation make the response easily understandable to regular English speakers.

critical_rules: Use the preview image only to predict the likely topic; once the recording starts, concentrate on listening and note taking.
Listen for the lecture's structure rather than trying to record every word.
Capture the topic, two or three main points, important relationships, and a possible conclusion.
Write notes as keywords, symbols, arrows, abbreviations, numbers, and short phrases rather than complete sentences.
Do not stop listening mentally when a word is unclear or unfamiliar; continue because later information may explain it.
Use the 10-second preparation period to choose an opening sentence and arrange the notes into a logical order.
Begin speaking promptly after the microphone opens and avoid a long silent start.
Retell the lecture in connected sentences rather than reading a disconnected list of notes.
Prioritize clear main ideas over minor facts, names, dates, or examples that do not support the central message.
Balance all three scoring areas: accurate content, smooth fluency, and understandable pronunciation.

learning_goals: Identify the topic or central theme of a lecture after one listening.
Distinguish major supporting ideas from examples, repetition, and less important details.
Recognize relationships such as cause and effect, comparison, contrast, sequence, problem and solution, and example.
Use brief notes, symbols, abbreviations, arrows, and layout to preserve meaning efficiently.
Reconstruct notes into complete spoken sentences without trying to reproduce the lecture word for word.
Organize a response with a clear topic sentence, logically ordered supporting points, and a conclusion or implication where possible.
Continue listening calmly after missing a phrase or hearing unfamiliar vocabulary.
Use cohesive language to connect ideas naturally within a 40-second response.
Maintain a steady speaking rate with controlled pauses and clear phrase stress.
Evaluate a recorded response for content coverage, oral fluency, pronunciation, timing, and organization.

core_method.name: TOPIC–POINTS–LINK–CLOSE Method
core_method.summary: Build the retell from a small number of high-value notes. First identify the lecture topic, then select the strongest supporting points, explain at least one relationship between those points, and finish with the speaker's conclusion or overall implication. This method reduces memory pressure and produces a response that sounds like a coherent summary rather than a list.

steps.detail: Use the three-second preview to identify possible subject vocabulary, people, objects, places, processes, trends, or categories shown in the image. Make only a prediction and remain ready to correct it.
During the opening of the lecture, listen for the broad subject and the speaker's main purpose. Write one short topic label, such as 'HDI rankings' or 'Sputnik rocket development.'
Record two or three ideas that directly explain, develop, compare, or support the topic. Ignore repeated wording and decorative detail.
Use arrows and symbols to show cause, result, contrast, sequence, continuation, increase, decrease, or example. Relationships make the retell more meaningful than isolated facts.
Listen carefully near the end for a conclusion, recommendation, implication, final comparison, or summary statement.
Choose an opening sentence, arrange notes into a sensible order, select two or three cohesive devices, and decide where to finish.
Deliver the response in short sense groups: topic, first point, second point, relationship or example, and conclusion. Stress key content words and pause briefly between ideas.
After practice, check whether the response clearly communicated the topic, covered the major ideas, remained fluent, and finished within the available time.

core_method.formula: Topic sentence + Main point 1 + Main point 2 + Relationship or example + Conclusion or implication

techniques.name: Five-Box Note Map
techniques.purpose: To prevent excessive note taking and ensure that the response contains the information most useful for content scoring.
how_to: Divide the note area mentally into five positions: topic, point one, point two, relationship or example, and conclusion.
Write only one compact idea in each position.
Leave a box empty when the lecture does not provide that type of information.
Use the 10-second preparation period to read the boxes from left to right.
Convert each box into one spoken clause or sentence.
techniques.example: Topic: urban heat; P1: concrete absorbs heat; P2: fewer trees reduce cooling; Link: both raise city temperature; Close: green spaces can reduce effect.
techniques.why_it_matters: The map gives the response an immediate structure and reduces the risk of speaking from a page of scattered, unreadable notes.
techniques.common_error: Trying to fill every box with several details, which recreates the original problem of writing too much.

techniques.name: Keyword-and-Relationship Notes
techniques.purpose: To preserve meaning while writing much faster than full-sentence note taking.
how_to: Write nouns, main verbs, adjectives, numbers, and technical terms.
Remove articles, auxiliary verbs, and other grammar words unless they carry important meaning.
Use arrows for cause and result, plus and minus signs for advantages and disadvantages, and upward or downward arrows for changes.
Place related ideas close together on the page.
Expand the compressed notes into grammatical sentences while speaking.
techniques.example: gov't pol. → ↑ dev.; better roads + schools; rural areas benefit; result = higher participation.
techniques.why_it_matters: The technique frees attention for listening because the learner records ideas rather than transcribing language.
techniques.common_error: Creating abbreviations that are so unclear that they cannot be decoded during the 10-second preparation time.

techniques.name: Main-Idea Filter
techniques.purpose: To separate important lecture content from examples, repetition, side comments, and minor data.
how_to: Ask whether the detail explains the topic or merely illustrates it.
Give priority to ideas repeated, emphasized, contrasted, or summarized by the speaker.
Notice signposts such as 'the main point,' 'most importantly,' 'however,' and 'therefore.'
Record one representative example rather than every example.
Remove low-value notes during the preparation period.
techniques.example: If the speaker lists five countries to illustrate high HDI, note 'Norway/Iceland/Australia = high examples' rather than writing the entire list.
techniques.why_it_matters: A 40-second response cannot contain everything, so the learner must select information that best represents the lecture.
techniques.common_error: Retelling memorable numbers or names while omitting the main argument they were intended to support.

techniques.name: Calm-Recovery Listening
techniques.purpose: To stop one missed word or phrase from causing the learner to lose the next part of the lecture.
how_to: Mark an unclear section with a question mark instead of trying to solve it immediately.
Return attention to the speaker within one second.
Listen for restatement, definition, example, contrast, or consequence that may clarify the missing information.
Use the surrounding meaning to create a safe general statement.
Exclude uncertain details when they are not necessary for the central message.
techniques.example: If a technical term is unclear but the speaker explains that it measures national quality of life, note 'index measures quality of life' and continue.
techniques.why_it_matters: Losing one detail is manageable; losing the next twenty seconds because of worry can damage the entire response.
techniques.common_error: Mentally repeating the unclear sound while the lecture continues.

techniques.name: Ten-Second Launch Plan
techniques.purpose: To use the short preparation period efficiently and avoid hesitation when recording begins.
how_to: Circle or underline the topic.
Number the main points in speaking order.
Choose the exact first sentence before the microphone opens.
Select two or three linkers, such as 'first,' 'in addition,' and 'overall.'
Decide which optional detail to omit if time becomes short.
techniques.example: Opening selected in advance: 'The lecture explains how the Human Development Index is used to compare countries.'
techniques.why_it_matters: A prepared opening creates momentum, improves fluency, and makes it easier to continue through the rest of the notes.
techniques.common_error: Using all 10 seconds to add more notes and beginning the response without a clear first sentence.

techniques.name: Sense-Group Delivery
techniques.purpose: To improve oral fluency, intelligibility, rhythm, and control under time pressure.
how_to: Speak in meaningful chunks rather than one word at a time.
Pause briefly after complete ideas, not in the middle of noun phrases.
Stress topic words, key verbs, contrasts, numbers, and conclusions.
Use a slightly falling tone when completing a point.
Keep a steady pace instead of accelerating sharply near the end.
techniques.example: The lecture explains the Human Development Index // and how it compares countries. // It looks beyond income // by considering several measures of quality of life.
techniques.why_it_matters: Clear phrasing makes the response easier to understand and supports both fluency and pronunciation performance.
techniques.common_error: Speaking too quickly without phrasing, causing words to merge and key ideas to become unclear.

techniques.name: Safe Paraphrasing
techniques.purpose: To retell the lecture in the learner's own words without changing its meaning.
how_to: Keep essential technical terms that cannot be replaced safely.
Replace common verbs and phrases with familiar equivalents.
Change sentence structure while preserving the speaker's relationship between ideas.
Use general wording when an exact detail is uncertain.
Avoid adding opinions or explanations that were not present in the lecture.
techniques.example: Original idea: 'The design is almost indistinguishable from the earlier rocket.' Safe retell: 'The modern rocket remains extremely similar to the one used at the beginning of the space age.'
techniques.why_it_matters: Safe paraphrasing demonstrates understanding and helps the learner speak naturally rather than struggle to reproduce exact wording.
techniques.common_error: Replacing a precise idea with an inaccurate synonym or inventing a stronger claim than the speaker made.

worked_examples.title: Human Development Index
worked_examples.input: Lecture notes: 'HDI = ranks nations; published index; beyond income; 3 criteria; quality of life; Norway/Iceland/Australia high.'
worked_examples.decoding: The central topic is the Human Development Index. The essential message is that it compares countries using more than income. The three criteria are important, while the named countries function as examples of high-ranking nations.
worked_examples.plan: Open with the purpose of the HDI, explain that it goes beyond income, mention that it uses three quality-of-life criteria, give the country examples, and finish with its broader value.
worked_examples.model_answer: The lecture explains the Human Development Index and how it is used to rank countries. The speaker says that the index looks beyond national income and compares quality of life by using three main criteria. Countries such as Norway, Iceland and Australia are presented as examples of nations with high rankings. Overall, the lecture shows that development should be measured through several aspects of human well-being rather than through economic wealth alone.

annotations.part: The lecture explains the Human Development Index
annotations.comment: Introduces the topic immediately and clearly.

annotations.part: looks beyond national income
annotations.comment: Communicates the lecture's main contrast.

annotations.part: using three main criteria
annotations.comment: Includes an important structural detail without inventing the criteria.

annotations.part: Norway, Iceland and Australia
annotations.comment: Uses the examples briefly rather than allowing them to dominate the response.

annotations.part: rather than through economic wealth alone
annotations.comment: Ends with the broader implication of the lecture.

worked_examples.title: Sputnik and Soyuz Rocket Technology
worked_examples.input: Lecture notes: 'Sputnik → start space age; machine = Soyuz; carries crews → ISS; rear view nearly same as old rocket; Russians found design worked → continued.'
worked_examples.decoding: The topic is the continuity of Russian rocket technology from Sputnik-era development to the modern Soyuz system. The key supporting evidence is its continuing use for International Space Station missions and its visual similarity to the earlier rocket.
worked_examples.plan: State the historical topic, identify Soyuz and its present function, compare the old and modern designs, and conclude that successful technology was retained.
worked_examples.model_answer: The lecture discusses Sputnik and the rocket technology associated with the beginning of the space age. The speaker identifies the modern vehicle as a Soyuz rocket, which is still used to transport crews to the International Space Station. An important point is that the back of this rocket looks almost the same as the rocket used around half a century earlier. The lecture therefore suggests that Russia developed an effective design and continued using the same basic technology because it remained reliable.

annotations.part: associated with the beginning of the space age
annotations.comment: Provides historical context without unnecessary dates.

annotations.part: transport crews to the International Space Station
annotations.comment: Includes the rocket's modern purpose.

annotations.part: looks almost the same
annotations.comment: Paraphrases the comparison accurately.

annotations.part: continued using the same basic technology
annotations.comment: Connects the historical and modern points.

annotations.part: because it remained reliable
annotations.comment: Expresses the lecture's implied explanation cautiously and logically.

worked_examples.title: Urban Heat Islands
worked_examples.input: Practice lecture: Cities are often warmer than surrounding rural areas. Concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night. Tall buildings can restrict airflow, while limited vegetation reduces shade and evaporative cooling. Planting trees and creating green roofs can reduce the effect.
worked_examples.decoding: The lecture follows a problem–causes–solution structure. The topic is urban heat islands. The main causes are heat-absorbing surfaces, restricted airflow, and insufficient vegetation. The conclusion recommends urban greenery.
worked_examples.plan: Name the phenomenon, present the major causes in a logical group, explain the result, and finish with the proposed solutions.
worked_examples.model_answer: The lecture explains the urban heat-island effect, in which cities become warmer than nearby rural areas. Concrete and asphalt absorb heat and release it slowly, while tall buildings can reduce airflow. The problem is made worse by a lack of vegetation because cities receive less shade and natural cooling. The speaker concludes that planting more trees and introducing green roofs can lower urban temperatures and reduce the overall effect.

annotations.part: cities become warmer than nearby rural areas
annotations.comment: Defines the central phenomenon clearly.

annotations.part: Concrete and asphalt absorb heat
annotations.comment: Presents the first major cause.

annotations.part: tall buildings can reduce airflow
annotations.comment: Adds a second cause without overloading the sentence.

annotations.part: made worse by a lack of vegetation
annotations.comment: Shows the relationship between another condition and the main problem.

annotations.part: planting more trees and introducing green roofs
annotations.comment: Finishes with the lecture's recommended response.

worked_examples.title: Government Policy and Educational Access
worked_examples.input: Notes: 'gov't pol. → ↑ school access; roads + digital learning; rural students benefit; cost not ↑ greatly; result = participation + long-term dev.'
worked_examples.decoding: The notes describe a cause-and-effect lecture. Government policy improves access through infrastructure and digital learning. Rural students benefit, participation increases, and long-term development may follow.
worked_examples.plan: Introduce the policy topic, explain the two mechanisms, identify the beneficiary group, describe the result, and end with the long-term implication.
worked_examples.model_answer: The lecture focuses on how government policy can improve access to education. It explains that investment in transport infrastructure and digital learning can help students reach educational services more easily, especially in rural communities. These measures may expand access without producing a major increase in cost. As a result, more learners can participate in education, and the speaker links this wider participation to stronger long-term social and economic development.

annotations.part: government policy can improve access to education
annotations.comment: Expands the abbreviation into a complete topic sentence.

annotations.part: transport infrastructure and digital learning
annotations.comment: Reconstructs the two main mechanisms from short notes.

annotations.part: especially in rural communities
annotations.comment: Identifies the population that receives the greatest benefit.

annotations.part: without producing a major increase in cost
annotations.comment: Preserves the contrast contained in the notes.

annotations.part: social and economic development
annotations.comment: Ends with the wider implication rather than another small detail.

items.when_to_use: Use when the topic is clear and the lecture is primarily explanatory.
Use when the lecture describes a process, concept, cause, or academic idea.
Use for a direct opening when you can name the central subject precisely.

items.item: The main topic of the lecture is...
items.when_to_use: Use when you need a simple and reliable opening under time pressure.

items.item: The speaker examines the relationship between...
items.when_to_use: Use when the lecture compares two factors or explains how they influence each other.

items.item: First, the speaker points out that...
items.when_to_use: Use to introduce the first major supporting idea.
Use when selecting a high-value idea from several lecture details.
Use to add a second main point connected to the topic.
Use when moving to a separate but equally important supporting idea.
Use when the lecturer strongly stresses or repeats a point.
Use to introduce an effect or consequence.
Use when one development directly produces another.
Use when the speaker compares opposing ideas, groups, periods, or outcomes.
Use to introduce an important cause or explanation.
Use when two developments occur together or when adding a balancing point.
Use for one representative illustration from the lecture.

items.item: The speaker gives the example of...
items.when_to_use: Use when a named case, country, person, experiment, or event supports the main point.
Use to connect a general claim with supporting evidence.
Use when reporting data, a finding, or a claim without presenting it as your own opinion.

items.item: The image supports this idea by showing...
items.when_to_use: Use only when the image directly reinforces information stated in the lecture.
Use to summarize the central message in the final sentence.
Use when the lecture contains an explicit conclusion.
Use when the lecture suggests a broader consequence rather than stating a formal conclusion.

items.item: In summary, the key point is...
items.when_to_use: Use when time is nearly finished and you need a controlled closing.
Use when the final idea follows logically from the supporting points.

items.item: The speaker appears to suggest that...
items.when_to_use: Use when the implication is reasonably clear but not stated directly.
Use when you remember a topic or example but not every exact detail.
Use when you can identify the general example but are uncertain about a minor name or number.

items.item: The main idea is related to...
items.when_to_use: Use as a recovery phrase when the exact technical label is unavailable.

common_mistakes.mistake: Continuing to study the image while the lecture is playing.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Visual attention competes with listening attention, causing the learner to miss the speaker's topic, transitions, and supporting points.
common_mistakes.fix: Use the image only during the preview, then look mainly at the note area and listen actively.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing complete sentences during the lecture.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Full-sentence writing is too slow and may cause the learner to miss later ideas.
common_mistakes.fix: Write keywords, symbols, arrows, numbers, and abbreviated relationships that can be expanded during speaking.

common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The response becomes rushed, disorganized, and likely to omit the central message.
common_mistakes.fix: Prioritize the topic, two or three main points, one relationship or example, and a conclusion.

common_mistakes.mistake: Freezing after missing a word or unfamiliar term.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: The learner may lose several additional sentences while mentally replaying one unclear sound.
common_mistakes.fix: Mark the gap with a question mark, continue listening, and use later context to recover the meaning.

common_mistakes.mistake: Reading notes as a disconnected list.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: A list lacks grammatical structure, cohesive links, and natural phrasing, which weakens clarity and fluency.
common_mistakes.fix: Convert each note group into a complete clause and connect the clauses with simple linkers.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using a memorized template that contains little lecture content.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Generic language consumes response time but does not communicate the actual ideas from the recording.
common_mistakes.fix: Use only a light structure for the opening and transitions, and fill most of the response with specific lecture content.

common_mistakes.mistake: Speaking extremely fast to include more information.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Rapid delivery reduces intelligibility, weakens stress and phrasing, and increases grammatical errors.
common_mistakes.fix: Choose fewer ideas and deliver them at a steady, understandable pace.

common_mistakes.mistake: Pausing for several seconds before starting.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: A delayed start wastes limited recording time and can disrupt fluency.
common_mistakes.fix: Prepare the exact opening sentence during the 10-second planning period.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding personal opinions or outside knowledge.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Extra information may be inaccurate or irrelevant and can replace important lecture content.
common_mistakes.fix: Report only the speaker's main ideas, examples, conclusions, and reasonable implications.

common_mistakes.mistake: Focusing only on content and ignoring pronunciation or fluency.
common_mistakes.why_it_hurts: Accurate ideas may still be difficult to understand when speech is hesitant, poorly phrased, or unclear.
common_mistakes.fix: Record practice responses and review content, fluency, and pronunciation as three separate performance areas.

time_budget.focus: Review the preview, recording, 10-second preparation, 40-second response, and the three scoring factors.
Identify topics, purposes, main ideas, and lecture structures without speaking.
Practise keywords, abbreviations, arrows, symbols, layout, and relationship marking.
Turn short note sets into complete, logically connected spoken summaries.
Practise sense groups, key-word stress, controlled pauses, clear endings, and a steady speaking rate.
Complete several attempts using the three-second preview, one listening, 10-second planning, and 40-second speaking pattern.
Review recordings for content coverage, organization, fluency, pronunciation, timing, and one priority improvement.

drills.name: Five Notes Only
drills.instructions: Listen to a short lecture once and write exactly five notes: topic, two main points, one relationship or example, and one conclusion. Deliver a retell using only those notes.

drills.name: Abbreviation Builder
drills.instructions: Create and repeatedly use a personal shorthand set for government, increase, decrease, cause, result, comparison, advantage, disadvantage, with, without, number, and approximately.

drills.name: Miss-and-Move Drill
drills.instructions: During a practice recording, deliberately ignore one difficult word. Continue listening and later summarize the passage without trying to recover that exact word.

drills.name: Topic Sentence Sprint
drills.instructions: Listen to the first 15 to 20 seconds of several short talks and produce one accurate opening sentence for each within five seconds.

drills.name: Relationship Hunt
drills.instructions: Listen for cause, result, contrast, sequence, problem, solution, and example. Mark each relationship with a symbol and explain it aloud in one sentence.

drills.name: Notes-to-Grammar Drill
drills.instructions: Take compressed notes such as 'policy → access ↑; rural stdnts benefit' and expand each set into one or two complete grammatical sentences.

drills.name: Thirty-to-Forty-Second Build
drills.instructions: Begin with a controlled 25-second retell containing only the topic and two points. Gradually add a relationship and conclusion until the response lasts approximately 35 to 40 seconds.

drills.name: One-Take Recording Review
drills.instructions: Record one response without restarting. Listen once for content, once for fluency, and once for pronunciation, then repeat the task with only one targeted correction.

practice_plan.routine: For each practice lecture, follow the same cycle: preview the image for three seconds, listen once, create a five-part note map, use 10 seconds to select the opening and speaking order, deliver a 35-to-40-second retell, and review the recording using three headings—Content, Fluency, and Pronunciation. Record one specific improvement target before attempting the next lecture.

mastery_checklist: I can identify the lecture topic during its opening section.
I can recognize two or three main supporting ideas after one listening.
I can distinguish main ideas from examples, repetition, and minor details.
I can mark cause, result, contrast, sequence, and other relationships in my notes.
I can use a consistent set of abbreviations and symbols that I can decode quickly.
I can continue listening calmly after missing a word or phrase.
I can use an image to predict the topic without allowing it to distract me during the recording.
I can prepare a clear opening sentence within the 10-second planning period.
I can organize my retell as topic, supporting points, relationship or example, and conclusion.
I can speak from notes without reading them as a disconnected list.
I can maintain a steady and natural speaking rate for approximately 35 to 40 seconds.
I can use clear phrase stress, understandable pronunciation, and controlled pauses.
I can finish with a conclusion or implication instead of stopping suddenly.
I can evaluate my response separately for content, oral fluency, and pronunciation.
I can complete the full preview, listening, planning, and response sequence under timed conditions.
strategy_notes: The first sentence should identify the lecture topic directly; avoid a long generic introduction.
The opening and closing of a lecture often contain the highest-value information, so listen carefully at both points.
Repeated or strongly emphasized ideas are usually more important than isolated facts.
A single meaningful relationship between ideas can improve the retell more than several unrelated details.
Keep essential technical vocabulary when paraphrasing it would risk changing the meaning.
Use broad but accurate wording when a minor name, figure, or technical term is uncertain.
One clear example is normally enough to demonstrate supporting detail in a short response.
Do not apologize, correct yourself repeatedly, or explain that you missed information.
A short pause between ideas is useful; repeated hesitation inside phrases is not.
Aim to finish naturally before the response window closes rather than filling every available second with weak content.
Use recordings to identify repeated habits such as rushing, monotone delivery, excessive fillers, weak endings, or unreadable notes.
Change only one major weakness at a time during practice so that improvement remains measurable.

metadata.estimated_study_time: About 2 hours in one focused session, followed by additional timed retell and feedback practice.
